title: Decimals: Multiply & Divide
subtitle: Adding said line up the points. Multiplying says the opposite.
objectives: Multiply decimals by counting the decimal places in both factors
Multiply and divide decimals by 10, 100 and 1000
Divide a decimal by a whole number
Divide by a decimal by making the divisor a whole number
Explain why multiplying by less than 1 makes a number smaller
Estimate first to check the decimal point is in the right place

cards.title: Forget everything about lining up the points
cards.text: Adding decimals needed the points stacked. Multiplying does not care where they are. That contradiction is where most marks get lost.

cards.title: Ignore the points, then count them
cards.text: Two steps, in this order, every single time.
points: **Step 1:** multiply as if there were no decimal points at all.
**Step 2:** count the decimal places in *both* numbers.
**Put that many places** into your answer.

cards.title: Three worked examples
cards.text: Tap each one. Watch the places get counted, not aligned.

cards.title: Estimate before you trust the answer
cards.text: Round both numbers and multiply those in your head. It will not give the answer, but it tells you where the point goes.
points: **Every decimal-point mistake** is caught by this in two seconds.

cards.title: Every damage number you have seen is this
cards.text: Games multiply damage by decimals constantly. That is what a crit multiplier and a resistance stat both are.
points: **You already read these fast.** Same skill.

question.text: You do 40 damage with a ×0.25 multiplier. What lands?
question.explain: 40 × 0.25 = 10. A quarter of the damage. Multiplying by less than 1 always shrinks it.

cards.title: Times 10, 100, 1000 — move the point right
cards.text: No working needed for these. Count the zeros, move the point that many places to the right.
points: **More zeros, more places.** That is all it is.

cards.title: A 7 is not a bit worse than a 6
cards.text: Earthquake magnitude is a powers-of-ten scale. One step up is ten times the shaking, not one more unit.
points: **Energy goes up about 32 times** per step.

question.explain: 260. Two zeros means the point moves two places right, so you add a zero to fill the gap.

cards.title: Multiplying does not always make it bigger
cards.text: You have believed this since Grade 1 and it is about to stop being true.
points: **Below 1 shrinks. Above 1 grows. Exactly 1 does nothing.**

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Multiplying done. Part 2 is dividing, which has one extra move and one matching trap. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Two cases, and only one is hard
cards.text: Dividing by a whole number is normal division. Dividing by a decimal needs one move first, and then it is also normal division.

cards.title: Dividing by a whole number
cards.text: Set it out as usual. The decimal point in the answer sits directly above the one inside.
points: **Add zeros on the end if you need them.** 7 becomes 7.00.
**Nothing new here.** It is the division you already do.

question.explain: 96 ÷ 4 = 24, and the point stays put, so 2.4. Estimate: 10 ÷ 4 is about 2.5.

cards.title: Dividing BY a decimal
cards.text: You cannot divide by 0.4 easily. So make it a whole number first — and do the same thing to the other number.
points: **4.8 ÷ 0.4** — move both points one place right.
**It works because you scaled both sides equally.**

cards.title: Protein per kilogram is a division problem
cards.text: Sports nutrition guidance is given per kilogram of bodyweight, so the number is always a decimal.
points: **Around 1.6 g of protein per kg** is the usual figure for athletes.
**At 42.5 kg that is 68 g a day.**
**Guidance you cannot do the sum for** is useless to you.

question.explain: Move both points one place: 35 ÷ 5 = 7. Ask yourself how many halves fit into 3.5 — seven.

cards.title: Divide by 10, 100, 1000 — move the point left
cards.text: The mirror image of multiplying. Same count of zeros, opposite direction.

cards.title: How many times further is Jupiter?
cards.text: Distances from the Sun are measured in astronomical units. Earth is 1 AU by definition.
points: **Mars is about 1.52 AU.** Jupiter is about 5.2 AU.
**Jupiter is roughly three and a half times further out** than Mars.
**"How many times bigger" is always a division.**

question.explain: 0.074. Two zeros, so two places left, and a zero has to appear to fill the gap.

cards.title: Dividing does not always make it smaller
cards.text: The matching pair to the multiplying trap. Dividing by something less than 1 makes the answer bigger.
points: **Because you are asking how many halves fit into 6.**
**Say the question out loud** and it stops being strange.

terms.def: One of the numbers being multiplied. 1.2 and 0.3 are both factors.
The number being divided. In 4.8 ÷ 0.4, it is 4.8.
The number you are dividing by. In 4.8 ÷ 0.4, it is 0.4.
A digit after the point. 3.14 has two decimal places.
A rough answer from rounded numbers, used to check the point is right.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Multiply:** ignore the points, then count them in both.
**Divide by a decimal:** move both points until the divisor is whole.
**× and ÷ by 10s:** right for times, left for divide.
**Below 1 flips your instincts.** Estimate first, every time.

quiz.objective: Multiply decimals by counting the decimal places in both factors

quiz.explain: 125 × 4 = 500, with two decimal places, so 5.00. A quarter more than 1, four times, is 5.
quiz.objective: Multiply decimals by counting the decimal places in both factors

quiz.explain: Two zeros, so the point moves two places right. 503.
quiz.objective: Multiply and divide decimals by 10, 100 and 1000

quiz.explain: Three zeros, so three places left. 0.0625.
quiz.objective: Multiply and divide decimals by 10, 100 and 1000

quiz.explain: 84 ÷ 7 = 12, and the point stays above where it was, so 1.2.
quiz.objective: Divide a decimal by a whole number

quiz.text: What is the first thing you do with 6.3 ÷ 0.9?
options: Move both decimal points one place right
Move only the 0.9 point one place right
Move both points one place left
quiz.explain: Both, or the answer changes. It becomes 63 ÷ 9 = 7.
quiz.objective: Divide by a decimal by making the divisor a whole number

quiz.explain: 45 ÷ 5 = 9. Nine halves fit into 4.5, which is why the answer got bigger.
quiz.objective: Divide by a decimal by making the divisor a whole number

quiz.text: Multiplying a number by 0.75 always makes it smaller.
quiz.explain: True, for any positive number. 0.75 is less than 1, so you end up with three quarters of it.
quiz.objective: Explain why multiplying by less than 1 makes a number smaller

quiz.text: Dividing a number by 0.25 makes it smaller.
quiz.explain: False. It makes it four times bigger, because you are counting how many quarters fit inside.
quiz.objective: Explain why multiplying by less than 1 makes a number smaller

quiz.explain: About 4 × 5 = 20, so the answer sits near 20. Only 19.89 does.
quiz.objective: Estimate first to check the decimal point is in the right place

quiz.text: A car uses 1.6 litres of fuel per lap. How many litres for 12 laps?
quiz.explain: 16 × 12 = 192, with one decimal place, so 19.2 litres. Estimate: about 1.5 × 12 = 18.
quiz.objective: Multiply decimals by counting the decimal places in both factors

quiz.text: Put these in order of size, smallest first.
quiz.explain: 2, then 4, then 8, then 16. Below 1 shrinks when you multiply and grows when you divide.
quiz.objective: Explain why multiplying by less than 1 makes a number smaller

teacher.summary: Week 5 Math covers multiplication and division of decimals, completing the four operations begun in Weeks 3 and 4. It is built around the contradiction that causes most of the lost marks: addition requires the points aligned, multiplication requires them ignored and then counted. The decimalPlaces figure is deliberately the companion to the decimalColumns figure from Week 3, so the two rules stay separate rather than blurring into one half-remembered instruction. Estimation is introduced as a habit rather than a topic, because it is the only reliable defence against a misplaced decimal point. The two traps — multiplying by less than 1 shrinks, dividing by less than 1 grows — are taught as a matching pair, since meeting them separately is what makes them feel arbitrary.
discussion: Ask him why 8 × 0.5 is smaller than 8. If he can say 'because I'm taking half of it', the rule is understood rather than memorised.
Ask him to estimate before every answer for one session. It is the single habit that raises a decimals mark the most.
Ask why you have to move both decimal points when dividing by a decimal. Moving only one changes the answer, and he can test that himself.
Ask him to invent a question where multiplying makes a number smaller. Writing one is harder than answering one.
teacher.extension: Give him a real receipt or a fuel bill and ask him to check the arithmetic, estimating first. Real numbers are untidy in a way textbook questions are not, and the estimate is what makes them manageable.
misconceptions: 'Line up the decimal points.' That is addition and subtraction. For multiplication you ignore the points and count them at the end.
'Multiplying always makes a number bigger.' Multiplying by anything less than 1 makes it smaller. This is the most common Grade 6 error.
'Dividing always makes a number smaller.' Dividing by less than 1 makes it bigger, because you are counting how many small parts fit inside.
'When dividing by a decimal, move the point in the divisor only.' Both numbers move the same number of places, or the answer is wrong.
